title: How to lead a happy life (The Educated Barbarian: Seneca analysis, part. 2)
summary: NH reads Seneca's chapter on virtue as the basis of happiness. Virtue is internal, open to everyone and unaffected by status or misfortune; virtue signalling is its opposite. He describes two people he met who radiated virtue, sets contemplation before action, and opposes virtue to pleasure. The next Educated Barbarian cycle is announced: Nietzsche, Dostoevsky and Jung.
claims: Virtue exists above humans in nature, so it is immortal and open to anyone
Being good at a job or having status doesn't make you virtuous; virtue is internal
Virtue signalling puts reputation over the soul and closes the door to real virtue
Only internal degradation can remove virtue; external hardship can't
You do virtuous acts because you are virtuous, not the reverse
Age doesn't bring virtue; many 50-60-year-olds are as childish as kids
His boxing coach at 19, aged 55-60, radiated virtue and something like enlightenment
Truly virtuous people dislike being praised for it
Morals produced religion, not the other way around; humans naturally revere virtue
People who most loudly claim moral virtue often turn out the worst
No one is born evil (rare exceptions aside); everyone has an inner light of virtue they can choose to follow
People rename vice as virtue to live with themselves; he gives sex work as an example
Merely contemplating virtue is already worth something and makes virtue attainable
Every action starts as contemplation; achieving what you contemplate fuels more action
The most frightening-looking things are often the least to be feared; the real threats pull you away from virtue
Insecure people aren't virtuous; they lash out because they lack self-belief
Equating pleasure with virtue (hedonism) is for fools ruled by instinct
Next cycle: Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals, then Dostoevsky and Jung
